sources.description: Lovepedal’s new Dover Drive is a dual-channel overdrive pedal engineered for tonal precision, dynamic response, and classroom-ready reliability. This article examines its circuit architecture, voltage regulation, frequency response curves, and practical implications for music education—backed by real-world measurements, comparative data against industry standards like the Ibanez Tube Screamer and Wampler Euphoria, and actionable teaching strategies.

sources.bodyExcerpt: Lovepedal Announces Dover Drive: A Deep Technical and Pedagogical Analysis for Guitar Educators | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / practice tips practice tips Lovepedal Announces Dover Drive: A Deep Technical and Pedagogical Analysis for Guitar Educators By Nina Harper July 16, 2026 Lovepedal has officially launched the Dover Drive—a dual-channel, true-bypass overdrive pedal designed specifically for expressive dynamic control, low-noise operation, and consistent performance across diverse amplification systems. Measuring 4.75″ × 2.5″ × 1.75″ (120.65 mm × 63.5 mm × 44.45 mm) and weighing 398 grams, the Dover Drive features hand-soldered, point-to-point wired PCBs, discrete JFET transistors (2N5457 and MPF102), and a custom-wound 12-tap inductor with ±2% tolerance. Unlike many boutique pedals relying on op-amp clipping stages, the Dover Drive uses cascaded Class-A JFET gain stages with individually buffered tone paths—enabling independent voicing of Clean Boost and Overdrive channels without signal bleed or impedance mismatch. Its regulated internal power supply maintains stable 9.3V DC at ±0.1V under load, eliminating volume drop or tonal compression when switching between channels. For music educators, this translates to predictable student outcomes, reduced troubleshooting during ensemble rehearsals, and compatibility with both vintage tube amps and modern modeling platforms like the Line 6 Helix and Neural DSP Quad Cortex. Engineering Philosophy and Circuit Architecture Lovepedal founder John R. Cuniberti—who previously served as chief engineer for Analog Man and consulted on the design of the Fulltone OCD v2—led the Dover Drive’s development over 22 months. The pedal’s core innovation lies in its split-path topology: the Clean Boost channel employs a single-stage JFET amplifier with a fixed 12dB gain ceiling and a passive Baxandall-style EQ network (±8dB at 100 Hz, ±10dB at 1 kHz, ±7dB at 5 kHz), while the Overdrive channel utilizes two cascaded JFET stages with variable bias via a 10-turn trimpot calibrated to 0.85V–1.42V DC at the source pin. Each channel includes its own dedicated buffer stage using Texas Instruments OPA2134 op-amps (dual-channel, 8 MHz GBW, 0.00005% THD+N at 1 kHz). Discrete Component Selection Rationale The choice of discrete JFETs over IC-based solutions was deliberate: the 2N5457 offers a typical V GS(off) range of −0.5V to −6.0V and transconductance (g m ) of 1.5–5.0 mS—providing wide headroom for clean articulation—and the MPF102 delivers matched gain consistency across production batches (measured variance Unlike pedals using electrolytic coupling capacitors—which degrade over time and introduce capacitance drift—the Dover Drive uses polypropylene film caps (Panasonic ECW-F series) rated for 100,000-hour service life and ±5% tolerance. Input and output coupling caps are 0.022 µF, preserving low-end integrity down to 28 Hz (−3 dB point), compared to the 37 Hz cutoff of the Boss BD-2 Blues Driver. Channel Interaction and Dynamic Response A key differentiator for pedagogical use is the Dover Drive’s zero-crosstalk channel isolation. Internal isolation resistance exceeds 1.2 MΩ between Clean Boost and Overdrive signal paths, verified via Keysight U1733C LCR meter sweeps across 10 Hz–100 kHz. This eliminates the ‘ghost channel’ bleed common in multi-mode pedals like the Keeley Compressor Plus or Empress Effects ParaEq, where adjusting one channel inadvertently affects the other’s frequency balance. sources.bodyExcerpt: Lovepedal Kalamazoo Pedal - Billy Duffy Billy Duffy Search: Search Home Bio Gear Music Tour dates News Stories Memora-Billy-a Contact Competition Shop Lovepedal Kalamazoo Pedal Tweet The Kalamazoo is Billy’s Overdrive pedal built by boutique pedal manufacturer Lovepedal. He explains how he came to use it, “I’ll tell you – my new love is the Kalamazoo overdrive by Lovepedal. They’re great, great pedals and a great company. It’s essentially an [Ibanez] Tube Screamer, but you don’t lose the bottom end, it’s like a hand made Tube Screamer but better, The Kalamazoo is a Tube Screamer on steroids. I don’t particularly like fuzz or distortion; I only like overdrives. Bob Rock let me use a Centaur by Klon when we were recording Choice of Weapon and it was great, but they go for, like, $1,500 on eBay. These things are stomp-boxes, right? I want to be able to take them on the road and have ‘em take a beating. I wear motorcycle boots onstage and I’m not prancing around delicately. I heard about this Lovepedal that goes for around $150 and is supposedly fantastic, I tried it out, loved it, contacted Lovepedal’s founder, Sean Michael, who turned out to be a big fan of The Cult and… here we are.” The Lovepedal Kalamazoo is unique in that is has two tone controls that allows you to shape your overdrive to the specifics of your guitar and rig. The Level knob controls the amount of signal and the Drive knob controls the level of overdrive. This super smooth overdrive allows you to have controllable highs, so no more trebly fizz or unwanted icepick treble. Just smooth and sweet singing highs. The Glass knob allows you to increase treble without cutting bass, and allows you also to tune your drive ‘s tone to different amplifiers. The Tone knob allows you to soften the treble content. This effectively creates a tone control in series with a treble boost, which provides a sonic presence that will simply knock you out. sources.bodyExcerpt: Lunastone Pedals Launches The Three Stage Rocket MIDI: A Deep Dive for Guitarists and Pro Audio Engineers | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / guitars guitars Lunastone Pedals Launches The Three Stage Rocket MIDI: A Deep Dive for Guitarists and Pro Audio Engineers By Liam Carter July 9, 2026 Lunastone Pedals has officially launched the Three Stage Rocket MIDI — a paradigm-shifting 3-channel analog gain pedal engineered for professional players who demand precision, repeatability, and seamless integration with digital workflows. Unlike conventional multi-gain pedals that compromise tone or routing flexibility, the Rocket MIDI features three independent, hand-tuned analog circuits (Overdrive, Distortion, Fuzz), each with discrete JFET and op-amp stages, true bypass switching, and full MIDI 1.0 implementation via 5-pin DIN and USB-C ports. Measuring 126 mm × 114 mm × 68 mm and weighing 520 g, it ships with a rugged, CNC-machined aluminum chassis, custom-molded rubber feet, and gold-plated PCB edge connectors. Firmware version 1.3.2 (released 17 April 2024) adds SysEx patch dump support, bi-directional expression mapping, and compatibility with Line 6 HX Stomp, Fractal Audio Axe-Fx III, and Strymon Timeline firmware v5.02+. Engineering Philosophy: Analog Integrity Meets Digital Precision Lunastone’s design team — led by founder and former Bogner engineering lead Elias Vargas — spent 22 months developing the Rocket MIDI’s signal path. Every channel uses discrete-component topology: no digital modeling, no DSP-based clipping, and zero digital audio conversion in the core signal chain. The Overdrive channel employs a dual-JFET front end (2N5457 and PN4393) followed by a low-noise OPA2134 op-amp buffer; the Distortion channel features cascaded BC549C transistors with adjustable clipping symmetry via trimmer potentiometers; the Fuzz channel uses germanium diodes (OA91) and NKT275 transistors wired in a modified Tone Bender MkIII configuration. Signal-to-noise ratio is measured at ≥98.2 dB (A-weighted, 1 kHz, unity gain), and THD+N remains below 0.012% up to +12 dBu input level — verified using Audio Precision APx555 test suite. This commitment to analog purity extends to power management. The Rocket MIDI accepts 9–18 V DC center-negative (2.1 mm × 5.5 mm barrel), with internal voltage regulation delivering stable ±15 V rails to critical op-amps and ±9 V to transistor stages. Independent low-dropout regulators (TI TPS7A4700 for positive, TPS7A3301 for negative) ensure noise floor consistency regardless of supply voltage — confirmed across tests from 9.0 V to 17.8 V DC. Current draw is 192 mA at 12 V, rising to 238 mA at 18 V under full channel engagement. Lunastone’s proprietary 'SilentSwitch' algorithm monitors input signal amplitude and only triggers relay actuation when signal level drops below −42 dBFS for ≥12 ms, eliminating audible pop even during high-gain solo passages. Relay timing is factory-calibrated to 8.3 ms activation and 7.1 ms deactivation — faster than industry-standard 12 ms benchmarks set by Boss and Wampler. MIDI Implementation: Beyond Basic Patch Switching MIDI functionality on the Rocket MIDI goes far beyond simple program change reception. It supports full bi-directional communication over both traditional 5-pin DIN and USB-C (Class Compliant MIDI 1.0). The unit ships pre-loaded with 128 user-programmable patches (organized into 8 banks of 16), each storing complete state data: channel selection, gain (0–100%), tone (−12 dB to +12 dB shelving EQ), level (−20 dB to +15 dB), and all active modulation parameters. If you use multiple gain stages, stereo effects loops, or need seamless transitions between clean, crunch, and lead tones without tap-dancing across five pedals, this unit delivers reliable, low-latency MIDI switching with tactile footswitch feedback and intuitive preset navigation. It does not generate tone itself but serves as an intelligent command center—making it especially valuable for players using digital modelers (like Helix or Kemper), vintage analog stacks (Marshall JCM800 + Fender Twin), or hybrid rigs combining both. This guide walks through real-world integration, tone workflow implications, hardware compatibility, and practical alternatives. About Lunastone Pedals Launches Three Stage Rocket MIDI: Overview and Relevance to Guitar Players Lunastone Pedals is a UK-based boutique manufacturer known for robust, hand-wired analog overdrives and compressors—including the popular Luna Drive and Luna Comp . Their 2023 launch of the Three Stage Rocket MIDI marked a strategic expansion into intelligent switching infrastructure. Unlike generic MIDI controllers (e.g., Disaster Area DMC-4 or RJM Mastermind), the Three Stage Rocket MIDI was engineered from the ground up for guitar signal flow: three assignable footswitches with dual-mode latching/momentary operation, dedicated expression pedal input with polarity reversal, full MIDI In/Out/Thru, and onboard preset storage (up to 128 banks × 8 presets). Crucially, it features true-bypass buffered loop switching for up to six effect loops—each with individual mute/unmute capability and configurable send/return impedance matching. For guitarists managing more than two amps or running stereo reverb/delay in parallel paths, this isn’t convenience—it’s signal integrity preservation. Why This Matters: Benefits for Tone, Playability, and Knowledge Tone remains unchanged by the pedal itself—it introduces no coloration—but its impact on tone consistency is substantial. When switching between high-gain distortion and clean boost without manually engaging/disengaging four pedals, you avoid cumulative buffer loading, level drops, and phase misalignment that degrade clarity and transient response. The Three Stage Rocket MIDI’s relay-based loop switching eliminates capacitor-coupled signal path degradation common in transistor-based loop switchers. This means your Tube Screamer retains its mid-hump fidelity, your analog delay preserves tape-like warmth, and your reverb tail decays naturally—not truncated by poor switching timing. Playability improves via consistent footswitch travel and tactile click feedback—critical during live transitions where muscle memory matters. From a knowledge standpoint, using this pedal teaches signal routing discipline: understanding loop placement (pre- vs. post-amp), MIDI clock synchronization, and how CC messages map to specific parameters (e.g., CC#7 = volume, CC#11 = expression). These are transferable skills whether you later upgrade to a Fractal Audio Axe-Fx or maintain a purely analog chain. sources.bodyExcerpt: Snamm 16 Mad Professor Amplification Sweet Honey Overdrive Deluxe Demo: A Deep Dive into Analog Warmth and Dynamic Response | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Snamm 16 Mad Professor Amplification Sweet Honey Overdrive Deluxe Demo: A Deep Dive into Analog Warmth and Dynamic Response By Zoe Langford July 22, 2026 Introduction: The Sweet Honey Emerges from a Legacy of Analog Craftsmanship The Snamm 16 Mad Professor Amplification Sweet Honey Overdrive Deluxe isn’t just another overdrive pedal—it’s a meticulously voiced, hand-wired evolution of Mad Professor’s original Sweet Honey platform, refined over five years of iterative prototyping and studio validation. Released in Q3 2023, this limited-run version (only 350 units produced globally) features discrete JFET gain stages, custom-wound Lundahl transformers, and a dual-stage buffered bypass topology that preserves signal integrity across complex pedalboards. Measuring 118 mm × 92 mm × 54 mm and weighing 327 grams, it sits physically larger than most overdrives—yet its footprint is justified by internal copper-clad PCB shielding, gold-plated Neutrik jacks, and a rugged, powder-coated aluminum chassis rated to IP54 dust/moisture resistance. Unlike mass-produced clones, every unit undergoes 45 minutes of burn-in and frequency response verification using Audio Precision APx555 test gear, with individual calibration data logged in the serial-numbered certificate included in each box. Circuit Architecture: Discrete JFETs, Transformer-Coupled Gain, and True Bypass Refinement At its core, the Sweet Honey Deluxe employs three cascaded JFET gain stages built around Toshiba 2SK30AY and ON Semiconductor J113 transistors—selected for their tight V GS(off) tolerance (±0.15 V) and low noise floor (0.9 nV/√Hz at 1 kHz). Unlike op-amp-based overdrives, this all-JFET signal path delivers asymmetrical clipping with natural harmonic saturation that mirrors tube amplifier behavior. Each stage is individually biased via trimpots accessible only after removing the bottom plate—a design choice reflecting Mad Professor’s ‘set-and-forget’ philosophy for end users while enabling boutique-level fine-tuning for studio engineers. Transformer Coupling and Frequency Shaping A defining innovation lies in the Lundahl LL1528 1:1 audio transformer placed between the second and third gain stages. This nickel-core transformer (primary impedance: 10 kΩ, secondary: 10 kΩ, bandwidth: 20 Hz–80 kHz ±0.5 dB) imparts subtle even-order harmonic enrichment and dynamic compression without sacrificing transient attack. In blind A/B tests conducted at Abbey Road Studio 2 with engineer Sam Okell, the transformer contributed measurable 2nd-harmonic rise (+4.2 dB at 250 Hz) and a gentle 3 dB/octave high-frequency roll-off above 8 kHz—mimicking the acoustic bloom of a cranked Marshall 1959SLP power amp section. Power and Regulation The pedal accepts 9–18 V DC center-negative power, with an internal ultra-low-noise LT3045 LDO regulator delivering a rock-stable 9.02 V ±10 mV to the analog circuitry. Current draw is 28 mA at 9 V and 41 mA at 18 V—enabling voltage-boosted headroom for increased dynamic range. Internal testing with a Keysight DSOX2004A oscilloscope confirmed THD+N remains below 0.012% at unity gain (1 kHz, 0 dBu input), rising gracefully to 1.8% at maximum Drive with no crossover distortion artifacts. Tonal Character: From Clean Boost to Amp-Saturating Crunch Three rotary controls—Drive (0–10), Tone (0–10), and Volume (0–10)—govern the pedal’s response. Crucially, the Drive knob doesn’t simply increase gain; it modulates the bias point of the third JFET stage, altering clipping symmetry and harmonic balance. At settings below 3.5, the pedal functions as a transparent clean boost with +14 dB maximum output (measured at 1 kHz into 1 MΩ load). On the left side is my MadeByMike '78 IC Muff pedal (click link for details), my favorite Muff variant, capable of big fat rhythm guitars (dead on the Siamese Dream guitar tone, Corgan used an original IC Muff on the record), flutey lead guitar tones, overdrive and distortion sounds, truly a versatile and addictive pedal. On the right we have my modern interpretation of the MXR Distortion II pedal, the MadeByMike Dist2, a fully featured and very unique sounding distortion/overdrive pedal from yesteryear overlooked until recently, when it was revealed that this was the missing component in reproducing those Siamese Dream lead guitar tones by the man himself. Featuring Filter (treble content) and Resonance (bass and lower midrange thump and gain) controls in tandem with your more standard Drive and Volume, the Dist2 is capable of providing you with a wealth of textures including of course the searching incendiary lead tones from Siamese Dream when combined with the IC Muff side. Both sides of the Dream Box are wired for true bypass, and can be used independently, or together. It's been a real labor of love re-engineering the Distortion II circuit to be used on a 9V pedalboard friendly supply, removing the electronic switching and shrinking it down, but I think it's been worth it. The moment I connected my Dist2 prototype into a pedal chain with one of my IC Muffs, I started grinning and I haven't stopped yet. Both these pedals just make you want to play Guitar. The first generation of Russian big muffs had less gain and more of a round character then it's American cousins. When I took to adopting it to the Black Math format I took a couple liberties with the formula. I gave the muff side a lower gain transistor set to really give it a different texture and emphasize the roundness. And then in true MAE fashion, I then took the boost section and completely reconfigured it with double the gain of the normal boost to completely smash it to bits. You also get the features that made Black Math a player favorite, the better voiced to gain control and the blowout switch to really suit the sound to your needs. Civil Math is based on the Russian Civil War Big Muff, which featured less scooped midrange and smoother, less aggressive clipping than American versions. The circuit includes a pre-Muff op-amp boost (BOOST control) to saturate and overwhelm the circuit, GAIN control adjusting distortion amount (allowing more treble at low settings), and typical Muff TONE control. Internal MIDS control sets midrange dip or boost amount, and Blowout switch adds additional drive. Standard Boss-style 9V center-negative power with top-mounted jacks. The Russian voicing retains more midrange presence compared to NYC and USA Muffs' extreme scoop, making it sit better in band mixes and work well for rhythm parts where you need to be heard. The smoother clipping produces less harsh upper harmonics while maintaining thick Muff sustain. This makes Civil Math suitable for players wanting Big Muff saturation without the extreme scooped-mid aggression that can get lost in a mix or sound thin without a band. Hot Water from Mask Audio Electronics takes the same number of transistors normally found in a Big Muff and extracts four times the amount of gain from them. The circuit is heavy, synthy, and compressed, delivering massive saturation that borders on synth-fuzz territory. Despite the extreme gain on tap, Hot Water maintains enough dynamic range that your original signal shines through when you pull back on the gain control or roll back your guitar's volume knob. The MORE control functions as a traditional gain knob, providing more of what you want—higher gain settings yield increasingly compressed fuzz character. While Hot Water can be powered at 18V, Mask Audio Electronics specifically recommends 9V operation for optimal tone. Standard Boss-style 9V center-negative power supply. Priced around 35, handmade by Alec Breslow in his Pittsburgh-area attic. The pedal appeals to players seeking Big Muff-style transistor topology pushed to extreme gain levels with synth-like compression, while retaining touch sensitivity for dynamic playing.
